title: WHY MOSES AND ELIJAH APPEARED WHEN JESUS WAS TRANSFIGURED
paragraphs:
WHY MOSES AND ELIJAH APPEARED WHEN JESUS WAS TRANSFIGURED
They Were Not There to Make Jesus Look Important. They Were There Because Everything They Had Been Waiting For Was Standing Between Them.
There are moments in Scripture that feel almost too holy to interrupt with commentary.
This is one of them.
Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a mountain.
They think they are following their Rabbi.
They have no idea they are about to see behind the veil.
No crowds.
No Pharisees arguing.
No sick people pressing through the streets.
No demons screaming.
No ordinary afternoon in Galilee.
Just Jesus.
Then suddenly…
His appearance changes.
Matthew says:
“His face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light.”
— Matthew 17:2
Luke tells us that even the appearance of His face became different and His clothing flashed with brilliant whiteness.
And then two men appear beside Him.
Moses.
And Elijah.
That detail is so familiar to many Christians that we can read straight past it.
But stop there.
Why Moses?
Why Elijah?
Why not Abraham, the father of the covenant people?
Why not David, Israel’s great king?
Why not Isaiah, whose prophecies so vividly anticipated the suffering Servant?
Why did heaven place Moses and Elijah beside Jesus on that mountain?
And perhaps the even more important question is this:
What were they talking about?
Because Luke tells us.
And once you see the word Luke uses, the Transfiguration becomes even more breathtaking.
Moses and Elijah “appeared in glory, and spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem.”
— Luke 9:31
Our English word “decease” can make this sound as though they were simply discussing Jesus’ approaching death.
But Luke wrote something richer.
The Greek text says:
ἔλεγον τὴν ἔξοδον αὐτοῦ
elegon tēn exodon autou
They were speaking about His exodus.
The Greek noun is ἔξοδος — exodos.
Departure.
Going out.
Exodus.
Luke could have described Jesus’ death in other ways.
Instead, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, the Gospel uses a word that carries enormous biblical weight.
And standing beside Jesus while His coming “exodus” is being discussed is…
Moses.
The man God used in the first great Exodus.
Suddenly the mountain begins preaching.
Moses once stood before Pharaoh and watched God deliver His people from slavery.
Jesus was going to Jerusalem to accomplish the greater deliverance toward which the Exodus itself ultimately pointed.
Moses led Israel out from bondage under Pharaoh.
Jesus delivers sinners from bondage to sin and death.
Moses was associated with Passover blood placed upon Israelite homes.
Jesus would become the Lamb whose blood brings redemption.
Moses led people through the sea.
Jesus would pass through death itself and emerge victorious.
The first exodus brought an enslaved people out of Egypt.
Christ’s saving work brings enslaved sinners into reconciliation with God.
But there is something else you cannot afford to miss.
Moses did not finish Israel’s journey by bringing the people personally into the Promised Land.
He died outside it.
Yet centuries later, where does Scripture show Moses?
Standing in the land.
Beside Jesus.
Think about that.
The servant who once looked toward the promise from a distance is now standing beside the One in whom God’s promises find their ultimate fulfillment.
But why Elijah?
Because Moses and Elijah together carry enormous biblical significance.
Moses is inseparably associated with the Law.
Elijah stands as one of the great representatives of the prophetic tradition.
Together they naturally evoke what Scripture often describes as the Law and the Prophets.
And Jesus Himself had said:
“Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.”
— Matthew 5:17
There on the mountain, the Law is represented.
The Prophets are represented.
And standing between them is not another prophet competing for attention.
It is Jesus Christ.
The One to whom the Scriptures were pointing.
The One who fulfills rather than abolishes.
The One greater than Moses.
The promised Messiah.
The beloved Son.
But there is another layer.
Both Moses and Elijah had extraordinary encounters with God on mountains.
Moses ascended Sinai.
Elijah encountered God at Horeb.
Moses experienced divine revelation.
Elijah experienced divine revelation.
Both had ministries marked by confrontation, rejection, miraculous works, and covenant crisis.
And now both appear on another mountain.
But this time neither man is the center.
Jesus is.
That matters because Peter almost misses the point.
Peter sees Jesus, Moses, and Elijah and immediately starts talking.
That sounds painfully familiar.
God gives us a holy moment…
and we start trying to manage it.
Peter says:
“Lord, it is good for us to be here: if thou wilt, let us make here three tabernacles; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias.”
— Matthew 17:4
Three shelters.
One for Moses.
One for Elijah.
One for Jesus.
Perhaps Peter intended honor rather than equality. Luke even tells us that Peter did not fully understand what he was saying.
But before Peter can finish constructing his religious response, heaven interrupts him.
A bright cloud overshadows them.
Then comes the voice.
“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him.”
— Matthew 17:5
Read those final words again.
Hear Him.
The Greek is:
ἀκούετε αὐτοῦ
akouete autou
Listen to Him.
The Father does not say, “Listen to all three equally.”
He points the disciples to the Son.
Moses mattered.
Elijah mattered.
The Law mattered.
The Prophets mattered.
But neither Moses nor Elijah is Jesus.
And when the terrified disciples finally lift their eyes, Matthew gives us one of the simplest and most Christ-centered sentences in the entire scene:
“they saw no man, save Jesus only.”
— Matthew 17:8
Jesus only.
Moses disappears from view.
Elijah disappears from view.
Jesus remains.
Not because the Old Testament has become meaningless.
Exactly the opposite.
Its deepest purpose is being unveiled.
The Law was never supposed to become a substitute for Christ.
The prophets were never supposed to become substitutes for Christ.
The signs were never supposed to become substitutes for Christ.
The ceremonies were never supposed to become substitutes for Christ.
They were pointing beyond themselves.
Jesus later explained after His resurrection:
“These are the words which I spake unto you… that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me.”
— Luke 24:44
That is why the Transfiguration cannot be reduced to a spectacular supernatural event.
It is revelation.
It tells us something about who Jesus is.
And something about where He is going.
Because notice what happens immediately around this section of the Gospel story.
Jesus is moving toward Jerusalem.
Toward betrayal.
Toward humiliation.
Toward scourging.
Toward nails.
Toward blood.
Toward the cross.
The glory on the mountain does not cancel Calvary.
It prepares us to understand who is going there.
The One who will soon appear beaten and rejected is the beloved Son.
The One whose clothes will be stripped from Him is the One whose garments shone with heavenly brilliance.
The One men will mock as “King” possesses glory they cannot comprehend.
The One who will appear powerless before His executioners is willingly walking toward the saving mission He came to accomplish.
The mountain tells you that the cross will not happen because Jesus lost control.
He knows where He is going.
Luke says Moses and Elijah were discussing the exodus He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
Not merely endure.
Accomplish.
This is where the Transfiguration reaches into our own hearts.
Because most of us would choose the mountain.
We want Christianity filled with shining clothes, answered prayers, undeniable miracles, emotional worship, visible victories, and moments where God's presence feels unmistakably close.
We want glory.
We do not naturally want Gethsemane.
We do not naturally want surrender.
We do not naturally want repentance.
We do not naturally want the cross.
Peter wanted to remain on the mountain.
Jesus kept walking toward Jerusalem.
And maybe that exposes something in us.
We sometimes want a Jesus who makes life beautiful without being Lord over everything.
A Jesus who comforts but never confronts.
A Jesus who forgives but never commands repentance.
A Jesus who blesses our plans instead of crucifying our idols.
A Jesus who gives us heaven without asking us to follow Him through costly obedience.
But that Jesus is not the Jesus revealed in Scripture.
The glorious Christ on the mountain is the same Christ walking toward the cross.
Grace is free to the sinner.
But it was unimaginably costly to the Savior.
Maybe you have spent years trying to build your own little tabernacles.
One for success.
One for reputation.
One for money.
One for relationships.
One for religious appearance.
One for the version of yourself you desperately want everyone else to believe.
And somewhere among them…
you gave Jesus one too.
A place in your life.
But not the throne.
That is the scandal hidden inside respectable Christianity.
We can admire Jesus without surrendering to Jesus.
We can quote Jesus without obeying Jesus.
We can sing about Jesus while protecting the very sins He is calling us to confess.
We can know theology and still refuse repentance.
We can appear spiritually alive while quietly starving inside.
Then heaven speaks over all our noise:
Hear Him.
Maybe that is what your soul needs today.
Not another motivational voice.
Not another personality.
Not another algorithm telling you what will finally make you enough.
Not another person promising that your deepest problem can be solved by becoming richer, prettier, stronger, more admired, more productive, or more successful.
Hear Him.
Jesus says:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
— Matthew 11:28
Hear Him.
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
— Mark 1:15
Hear Him.
“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.”
— John 14:6
Hear Him.
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
— John 6:37
That last promise is for the person who almost stopped reading because shame whispered that Christianity is for cleaner people.
It is not.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people have finally earned God.
It is the announcement that God has acted in Christ to save sinners who could never rescue themselves.
You may have wrecked things.
You may have betrayed someone.
You may be carrying secret lust.
Secret bitterness.
Secret addiction.
Secret pride.
Secret unbelief.
You may know how to smile at church while privately wondering whether God could still want you.
You may have promised Him a hundred times that you would change.
Then failed again.
And again.
And again.
Do not mistake grace for permission to remain in darkness.
Jesus does not expose sin because He enjoys crushing sinners.
He calls sinners out of darkness because He came to save.
Repentance is not paying Jesus back.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who paid what you could never pay.
The cross means your sin is more serious than modern culture wants you to believe.
And grace means Christ is more merciful than your shame wants you to believe.
That is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement.
Resurrection.
Not reputation management.
Redemption.
Not hiding the scandal.
Grace rewriting what sin tried to destroy.
And this is why the Transfiguration matters so deeply.
Moses and Elijah appear.
The Law and the Prophets bear witness.
The Father speaks.
The disciples fall down.
And when they look again…
Jesus remains.
Eventually Moses cannot save you.
Elijah cannot save you.
Your pastor cannot save you.
Your church attendance cannot save you.
Your Christian vocabulary cannot save you.
Your charitable giving cannot save you.
Your parents’ faith cannot save you.
Your religious content cannot save you.
Your ability to look holy cannot save you.
Jesus saves.
And the Jesus revealed on that mountain did not remain safely inside glory.
He descended.
He continued toward Jerusalem.
He went toward the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day He rose.
The Transfiguration therefore gives us a glimpse of glory before the horror of Golgotha, but resurrection tells us Golgotha was never the end.
Peter would later remember that mountain.
Years afterward, he wrote that he and the other apostles had been “eyewitnesses of his majesty” and recalled the voice that came from the “excellent glory” declaring Jesus the beloved Son.
Peter never forgot.
How could he?
He had seen Moses.
He had seen Elijah.
He had seen the face of Jesus shine.
He had heard the Father speak.
Yet perhaps one of the greatest lessons of the mountain was learned when the spectacle ended.
Because eventually the cloud disappeared.
The voice became silent.
Moses was gone.
Elijah was gone.
And there stood Jesus.
Sometimes faith feels like the mountain.
Sometimes faith feels like the valley afterward.
Sometimes you feel God's presence intensely.
Sometimes you pray and feel nothing.
Sometimes worship brings tears.
Sometimes your Bible feels alive.
Sometimes you read the same page three times because your exhausted heart can barely concentrate.
Do not build your faith upon the intensity of the moment.
Look to Christ.
When the emotional experience fades…
Jesus remains.
When people disappoint you…
Jesus remains.
When your plans collapse…
Jesus remains.
When temptation returns…
Jesus remains.
When shame brings up your past…
Jesus remains.
When you have to repent again…
Jesus remains.
When death eventually comes knocking…
Jesus remains.
That is why this story is not merely about three glowing figures on a mountain.
It is about the supremacy of Christ.
The Law points toward Him.
The Prophets anticipate Him.
The Father identifies Him.
The cross reveals His saving mission.
The resurrection vindicates His victory.
And sinners are summoned to hear Him.
Who actually has your ear?
Jesus?
Or everyone else?
And if this article uncovered something you have been hiding, do not turn conviction into another fleeting emotional moment.
Bring it to Christ.
Confess it.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
There is grace for the ashamed.
There is restoration for the fallen.
There is hope for the exhausted believer who feels like the fire has almost gone out.
There is mercy for the prodigal coming home.
There is no scandal so powerful that the blood of Christ becomes powerless.
Someone reading your comment may realize they are not the only one fighting that battle.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
We are saved by grace, not by social-media engagement, financial support, religious performance, or works of righteousness we perform.
But if Christ has given you something worth hearing, there is something beautiful about refusing to keep it to yourself.
Someone may have stopped attending church.
Someone may believe their scandal disqualified them from grace.
Someone may need to hear about Jesus tonight.
Those gifts cannot be bought.
But glorifying God includes stewarding what He has entrusted to us for the advance of His truth.
The ministry is not the Savior.
The page is not the Savior.
The writer is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
That mountain settled the question.
Moses appeared.
Elijah appeared.
The Father spoke.
And then everyone else disappeared from view.
Jesus remained.
Maybe that is the message you need to carry with you long after you close this article:

When every lesser voice disappears, every false refuge collapses, every hidden scandal is exposed, and you finally have nothing left to hide behind—look up. Jesus is still there, and grace is still calling you home.
